THE TRIALS OF JESSE JAMES AND THE WIDOW WHIPPLE
JESSE JAMES AND THE WIDOW WHIPPLE
Northern District of New-York. To wit:
A CARD. – The proprietor of the New-York State Museum
When ordered to stand up she seemed to do it with difficulty, and was allowed to sit down. On being called on to plead, her voice was altogether inaudible—but it was a plea of Not Guilty.

There is a road, commonly called the Whitehall road, that comes down from the west about a quarter of a mile from Cherry Hill. The distance from the house to the woods is not over two hundred yards. Summoned a jury on that morning. Strang was on the jury. Thought he did not behave as the others did.
Judge John S. Van Rensselaer, sworn.
John S. Van Rensselaer, called again.
John S. Van Rensselaer called again, again.

Was one of the Grand Jury which found the bill against Strang. Strang was sworn and examined. In the first place they found a bill against Strang, before visiting him at all.—Then a committee of six called upon him, in order to find out what they could respecting the woman. Then the Grand Jury went in a body, and he was sworn and examined with regard to Mrs. Whipple altogether.
By the Court. As a Minister of the Gospel, and in that capacity alone, witness called on him. His advice to confess was dictated solely with reference to the good of his soul in another world.

Strang was sworn and examined with regard to the guilt of Mrs. Whipple, but no threats or inducements were offered to him to make any confessions relative to his own case. He was cautioned particularly by witness, that he need not say anything to incriminate himself.
John R. Williams, was thereupon called and sworn.

Four constables were then called to attend the jury, to keep them together—provide proper refreshments, & accommodations.—and bring them into court at 9 o'clock to-morrow morning—to which hour the court adjourned.

At 10 o'clock on the Sunday night after Strang's commitment, witness called to see him at his request. He then cautioned him that whatever he might say, must be said voluntarily. Does not recollect that he told Strang in express terms that he had nothing to expect by turning State's evidence, but said so in substance. He told him that he did not come there to obtain confessions. This was after Mr. Van Rensselaer had been there. Mr. Esleeck (now on the bench) was there.

A little before 4 o'clock in the afternoon, I called again at the livery stable for a horse and gig, but no gig being at home, I concluded to take a one horse wagon, and as there were strong indications of a storm, I asked Mr. Conklin for, and obtained the loan of an umbrella. I got into the wagon and drove to Mrs. Sanford's where I took Mrs Whipple from the stoop; then drove up the Troy road as far, as opposite the mansion of the honorable Stephen Van Rensselaer, where we turned to the left and went about seven miles to the Turnpike leading from Schenectady to Troy, at a place called the Four Corners.

From there I went to Meig's druggist store, purchased the sixpence worth of oil of spike, then called in at a tailor's shop, and inquired if I could get my pantaloons cut, and being answered that I could not, on account of its being so late, I hurried and run from there down South Market-street, turned into Church-street, to Ferry-street, then up Ferry-street to South Pearl-street, down South Pearl-street, to the city line, down the court yard at Cherry-hill.
—Four constables were then sworn to take charge of the jury, keep them together, and provide for them comfortable refreshment and lodging.
One of the Jurors having complained of illness, Doctors Ray and Townsend were called, and administered to him in the box.
—"Doctor" was a nick name which he had given Orton. Sometimes he was called Orton, and sometimes Doctor. Prisoner used to call him Doctor. Was in the habit of sending him to town with wood.

When Whipple was absent, thinks prisoner was called up once in the night to see little Abraham, her son, who slept below. Don't know who called her. She was gone perhaps half an hour. Mrs. Whipple did not tell witness what the matter was with Abraham.
At 6 o’clock the District Attorney moved the court that Jesse Strang be called to the stand to testify.

His Honor, Judge Duer then committed the cause to the jury, in an able and lucid manner. After a few prefatory remarks upon the enormity of the offense charged in the indictment, and laying down the law of murder, and the circumstances necessary to constitute the crime, such as the fact of killing with malice prepense, defining what is necessary to constitute such malice, &c., the Judge took up and examined the extraordinary chain of testimony which had been adduced by the prosecution, and traced it link by link, from the beginning to the final and fatal conclusion.
JOHN MONTEITH, JOSIAH NOYES, THEODORE STRONG, O.L. KIRKLAND, EBENEZER MALTBIE,

• May 7, 1827: John Whipple is assassinated at his Cherry Hill residence in Albany, New York. Shot through a window, the bullet enters his shoulder, severs an artery, and lodges in his lung. He dies almost instantly.
• May 8, 1827: Mayor James Stevenson offers a $500 reward for the apprehension of Whipple's killer.
• May 9, 1827: A funeral for John Whipple is held at Cherry Hill. Public reaction grows, and investigations are underway with examinations of witnesses.
• May 10, 1827: Governor DeWitt Clinton amplifies the reward for capturing the murderer.
• May 12-14, 1827: Jesse Strang, using the alias Joseph Orton, is arrested and examined. Initial evidence points to him as the primary suspect.
• May 15, 1827: Jesse Strang's true identity is revealed during further investigations.
• May 16, 1827: Reports emerge that Jesse Strang faked his death years earlier, building a history of deceit.
• May 17, 1827: Public speculation grows around the involvement of Elsie Whipple, though no conclusive evidence ties her directly to the crime.
• July 4, 1827: Emancipation Day in New York marks the abolition of slavery for those born before July 1799. This event sets a broader societal context, contrasting the grim events at Cherry Hill.
• July 24, 1827: Jesse Strang's trial begins in Albany. The court hears detailed accounts of his relationship with Elsie and the events leading to the murder.
• July 25, 1827: The district attorney presents the prosecution's case, asserting that Strang's relationship with Elsie motivated him to commit the murder.
• August 4, 1827: Jesse Strang confesses, offering a detailed account of his relationship with Elsie, her involvement, and the murder plot. This confession is later published.
• August 1827: Jesse Strang is sentenced to death. Public sentiment and the massive turnout for his execution highlight the societal impact of this case.
